claim: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that 90% of the nation's annual health-care spending is for people with chronic and mental-health conditions — the single largest category of U.S. health expenditure, which reached $4.5 trillion in 2022.

sources.label: CDC — National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, 'Health and Economic Costs of Chronic Conditions'
sources.quote: Ninety percent of the nation's $5.3 trillion in annual health care expenditures are for people with chronic and mental health conditions.

sources.label: CMS — 'National Health Expenditures 2022 Highlights'
sources.quote: U.S. health care spending grew 4.1% to reach $4.5 trillion in 2022.

sources.label: Cole Soiney / @rant.board, Instagram reel DZJJvUbtJ2g (June 3, 2026) — surfacing source

notes: The 90% chronic-and-mental-health figure is a verbatim CDC statement. Figure-year drift: the reel says $4.5 trillion, which matches CMS National Health Expenditures for 2022; the CDC page has since re-pegged the same 90% sentence to $5.3 trillion (later NHE data). Quote reflects the current CDC wording ($5.3T); the $4.5T (2022) is cited to CMS. The reel's added claim that '$1.8 trillion of that is federal' is NOT asserted here — the federal 'sponsor' share in 2022 CMS data was ~33%, roughly $1.5 trillion, so the $1.8T figure overstates the 2022 number and mixes years. A Feb-2026 fact-check flagged the popular framing of the 90% stat as contested even though CDC states it; documented here as CDC's own claim, attributed.
